catalog_quote: The distinction between long and short vowels is only clearly marked in words of Hindi origin. In pure Magar words there is very little distinction. The language in this respect also follows the usage of Tibetan. There are no peculiarities of accent beyond a slight drawl at the end of a sentence. The pronunciation is level and even, though somewhat indistinct, the words short and simple, and the general effect of the language on the ear is soft and musical.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Beames reports no noticeable word accent at all: pronunciation is 'level and even', the only prominence effect being a slight lengthening ('drawl') at the end of a sentence. No syllable is singled out as stressed, so no placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only qualification is the sentence-final drawl
new_statements.domain_note: Impressionistic 1870 remark in a 'Sounds' section, covering connected speech as a whole (sentence-final drawl is phrase-level); not a phonological analysis. The two 20th-century analyses that were readable are silent: Subba 1972 (p. 3) states outright that accent and intonation were not studied, and the SIL-based Magar note in Hale 1973 (pp. 18-19) discusses breathiness and pitch lowering but says nothing about stress. The modern reference grammar (Grunow-Hårsta 2008) could not be opened.
new_statements.first_reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.identity_note: Beames 1870 (the quoted source) worked with two Magar soldiers supplied by Jung Bahadur through the Kathmandu Residency and does not name their home district; Glottolog files the sketch under east2352 (Eastern Magar, mgp). The other readable descriptions are also eastern: Subba 1972's principal informant is from Rising, Tanahu; the SIL note in Hale 1973 (after Shepherd & Shepherd 1971) describes Yanchok, Tanahu; Baskaran 2009 describes Sikkim 'Mangari'.
